opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most interesting challenges right now, and also one of the hardest. The thing product designers have to internalize is that the underlying technology is moving incredibly fast. What a model can do today may be completely different six months from now. So if you design a product tightly around the current limitations, patching over every weakness, you can find that all that clever engineering becomes obsolete almost overnight when the next generation of models arrives.

So my advice would be to design for where the capabilities are going to be, not just where they are today. You have to anticipate the trajectory a bit, almost skate to where the puck is going, as they say. That means building products flexible enough that, when you swap in a more capable model, the product just gets better rather than breaking or needing to be rebuilt.

The other thing I'd say is that we're still very early in figuring out what the right interfaces even are. A lot of what we see today is chat boxes, which is a natural starting point, but I don't think that's the end state. As these systems become more multimodal, able to see and hear and understand the context you're in, and more agentic, able to actually take actions and plan over longer horizons, the interaction model changes. You might want something more like a universal assistant that's with you across devices and understands your world, rather than something you go and type a query into.

So designers should be thinking quite deeply about that: what does it mean when the AI can understand the physical world around you, remember context, and carry out tasks? That's a very different design space from traditional software, where everything is deterministic and you specify every pathway. Here you're designing around a system that has its own kind of capabilities and, to some degree, its own judgment. Getting the balance right between giving it autonomy and keeping the user in control, and making it trustworthy and reliable, is going to be a huge part of good product design going forward.

And honestly, I think the products that will really stand out are the ones that are built AI-first from the ground up, rather than bolting AI onto an existing workflow. It's a bit like the early days of mobile: the truly transformative apps weren't desktop websites shrunk down. They were things that only made sense because of what the phone could do. I think we'll see the same with AI.

r001.rationale: The response says current chat interfaces may not be the end state and describes future assistants, but it does not recommend simplifying the interaction layer so it does not obstruct model capabilities.

r002.rationale: It recommends designing for future capabilities and mentions six months, but does not recommend planning roughly a year ahead.

r003.rationale: It advises anticipating capability trends, but does not recommend assessing research trajectories to estimate when an infeasible product idea may become achievable.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing is to recognize that this is a very unusual moment for product design, because the underlying capability is shifting under your feet every few months. Normally when you design a product, the technology is relatively fixed and you're optimizing around its constraints. Here, the constraints you design around today may just dissolve by the next model generation. So I'd say the first principle is: don't over-engineer around the weaknesses of the current model. If you build a huge amount of scaffolding to compensate for something the model can't quite do yet, there's a good chance that scaffolding becomes dead weight, or even actively gets in the way, when the next version arrives. You want to build for where the trajectory is going, not just where it is today.

The second thing, and this is something we've thought about a lot at Google and DeepMind, is that the interface itself needs to change. For decades the paradigm has been that the human adapts to the machine. You learn the menus, you learn the commands, you learn where the buttons are. What these systems enable, really for the first time, is the machine adapting to the human. So an AI-first product shouldn't be a traditional app with a chat box bolted onto the side. It should start from the question of what the person is actually trying to accomplish, and then let the system figure out the steps. That's a fundamentally different way of thinking about design, and I think a lot of the current products are still in that transitional phase, somewhat awkwardly.

Then there's the question of trust and reliability, which I think is still underappreciated. These models are extraordinary, but they're not yet perfectly reliable, and the product has to be honest about that. You want to design systems where the model's uncertainty is surfaced in a useful way, where the user can verify things easily, and where mistakes are recoverable. In some sense that's good design regardless, but it matters more when the system is generating things rather than just retrieving them. I'm quite optimistic that reliability will improve dramatically, but I don't think designers should assume it away.

And finally, I'd say the most exciting products will be the ones that give people new capabilities rather than just automating old tasks. With AlphaFold, for instance, we didn't make an existing workflow slightly faster, we made something possible that essentially wasn't before. The same thing should be true in consumer products and in tools for scientists and creators. If you're a product designer right now, I'd think hard about what becomes possible when you have an assistant that can see, reason, plan, and act over long horizons, something closer to a true collaborator than a tool. We're not fully there yet, but we're on the path, and the best products will be designed with that destination in mind.

r001.rationale: It advises against building extensive scaffolding around current model weaknesses because that scaffolding may become dead weight or get in the way as models improve.

r002.rationale: It recommends designing for the direction of model progress rather than only current capabilities, but gives no roughly one-year-ahead time horizon.

r003.rationale: It refers generally to the technology’s trajectory, but does not recommend assessing research trajectories to judge when an infeasible idea may become technically achievable.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to design for where the technology is going, while being honest about what it can reliably do today. That’s quite a difficult balance, because the capabilities are changing so quickly. You can spend a year building around a limitation, and then the next generation of models makes that work unnecessary.

So I’d start with the user’s underlying goal. What are they trying to accomplish? If you had a really capable assistant working alongside them, how would that experience change? It probably wouldn’t just be the existing application with a chat box attached. You might rethink the whole interaction around expressing an intention, exploring possibilities, and then letting the system carry out some of the work.

But capability is only one part of it. The user needs to understand what the system has done, where it’s uncertain, and when they should intervene. As systems become more autonomous, those questions become more important. When should it ask you? Which actions should be reversible? How do you keep the person in control without making them approve every tiny step?

I’d build a very tight loop between the designers, the researchers, and actual users. You need to experiment with the models to understand what’s newly possible, and then watch people use the product to discover whether that possibility is actually useful. The technology is extraordinary, but making it feel simple and trustworthy is a substantial design problem in its own right.

r001.rationale: The response suggests rethinking interaction around user intentions and tasks, but does not clearly recommend simplifying the interaction layer so it does not obstruct model capabilities.

r002.rationale: It advises designing with future capabilities in mind and notes that models change quickly, but does not recommend planning roughly a year ahead.

r003.rationale: It recommends experimenting with models to discover what is newly possible, but does not describe assessing research trajectories to estimate when currently infeasible ideas will become achievable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to design for where the technology is going, while being very honest about what it can do today. That’s quite a difficult balance, because the models are improving so quickly. You don’t want to spend years building something whose main purpose is to work around a limitation that disappears with the next generation.

So I’d start with the user’s actual goal. What are they trying to accomplish, and what would a really helpful system do for them? Then work backwards from that, rather than taking an existing product and adding a chat box.

And I think the interface should evolve as the system becomes more capable. Initially, it might suggest things. Later, it might carry out a task, with your permission. But the user needs to understand what’s happening, be able to correct it, and know when it’s uncertain. Getting that relationship right—how much initiative the system takes, when it asks for help—is going to be a huge part of designing these products.
